heading: Introducing the technical controls
text: We have organised the requirements under five technical controls: 1. Firewalls 2. Secure Configuration 3. Security Update Management 4. User Access Control 5. Malware Protection

heading: Introducing the technical controls
text: As a Cyber Essentials scheme applicant organisation, it's your responsibility to make sure that your organisation meets all the requirements. You might also be required to supply evidence before your Certification Body can award certification at the level for which you’re applying.

heading: What you should do first
text: Establish the boundary of scope for your organisation, and then determine what is in scope within this boundary.

heading: What you should do first
text: Review each of the five technical control themes and the controls they embody as requirements.

heading: What you should do first
text: Take the necessary steps to ensure that your organisation meets every requirement it needs for the scope you have determined.

heading: Backing up your data
text: Backing up your data is not a technical requirement of Cyber Essentials. However, we highly recommend implementing an appropriate backup solution.

heading: Backing up your data
text: Backing up means creating a copy of your information and saving it to another device or to cloud storage (online).

heading: Backing up your data
text: Backing up regularly means you will always have a recent version of your information saved. This will help you recover quicker if your data is lost or stolen.

heading: Backing up your data
text: If automatic backups are available, you should consider turning them on. This will regularly save your information into cloud storage, without you having to remember.

heading: Backing up your data
text: If you back up your information to a USB stick or an external hard drive, disconnect it from your computer when a backup isn’t being done.

heading: Cyber Essentials scope overview
text: Your assessment and certification should cover the whole of the IT infrastructure used to carry out your organisation’s business, or if necessary, a well-defined and separately managed sub-set. Either way, you must clearly define the scope boundary, namely: the business unit managing it, the network boundary and physical location. You must agree the scope with the Certification Body before assessment begins.

heading: Cyber Essentials scope overview
text: A sub-set can be used to define what is in scope or what is out of scope for your Cyber Essentials certification.

heading: Cyber Essentials scope overview
text: Please note: Organisations that choose a scope which includes their whole IT infrastructure achieve the best protection and maximise their customers' confidence.

heading: Cyber Essentials scope overview
text: Where parts of an organisation’s infrastructure have been excluded from scope, you will need to justify the reason for a partial scope to your assessor.

heading: Cyber Essentials scope overview
text: The requirements apply to all devices and software in scope and which meet any of these conditions:

heading: Cyber Essentials scope overview
text: can accept incoming network connections from internet-connected devices

heading: Cyber Essentials scope overview
text: can establish outbound connections to devices via the internet

heading: Cyber Essentials scope overview
text: control the flow of data between any of the above devices and the internet

heading: Cyber Essentials scope overview
text: A scope that doesn’t include end-user devices isn’t acceptable.

heading: Cyber Essentials scope overview
text: If your organisation’s data or services are hosted on cloud services, these services must be in scope. Cloud services cannot be excluded from scope.

heading: Asset management and Cyber Essentials
text: Asset management isn’t a specific Cyber Essentials control, but effective asset management can help meet all five controls, so it should be considered as a core security function.

heading: Asset management and Cyber Essentials
text: Most business operations depend on some aspect of asset management, and cyber security shouldn’t be considered in isolation, or as the primary consumer of asset information. These functions include IT operations, financial accounting, managing software licences, procurement and logistics. They may not all need the same information, but there will be overlaps and dependencies between the respective requirements. Integrating and coordinating asset management across your organisation will help reduce or manage any conflicts between these functions.

heading: Asset management and Cyber Essentials
text: Effective asset management doesn’t mean making lists or databases that are never used. It means creating, establishing and maintaining authoritative and accurate information about your assets that enables both day-to-day operations and efficient decision making when you need it. In particular, it will help you track and control devices as they're introduced into your business.

heading: Asset management and Cyber Essentials
text: The NCSC has comprehensive guidance for organisations on asset management.

heading: Bring your own device (BYOD)
text: In addition to mobile or remote devices owned by the organisation, user-owned devices which access organisational data or services (as defined above) are in scope. However, all mobile or remote devices used only for the purpose of:

heading: Bring your own device (BYOD)
text: native voice applications

heading: Bring your own device (BYOD)
text: native text applications

heading: Bring your own device (BYOD)
text: multi-factor authentication (MFA) applications are out of scope.

heading: Bring your own device (BYOD)
text: Traditionally, user devices were managed centrally, which ensured consistency across the organisation. Certifying security controls in this way is more straightforward as there is a standard build or reference.

heading: Bring your own device (BYOD)
text: BYOD complicates matters, as users are given more freedom to ‘customise’ their experience making consistent implementation of the controls more challenging. Using the organisational data and services definitions to enforce strong access policies should remove some of this ambiguity.

heading: Bring your own device (BYOD)
text: For further information and advice on the use of BYOD please see the NCSC’s guidance.

heading: Home and remote working
text: Our default approach is that all corporate or BYOD home/remote working devices used for your organisation’s business are in scope for Cyber Essentials.

heading: Home and remote working
text: If your organisation gives the home/remote worker a router, that router is then also in scope.

heading: Home and remote working
text: All other routers are out of scope which means you need to apply Cyber Essentials firewall controls (such as a software firewall) on user devices.

heading: Home and remote working
text: If the home/remote worker is using a corporate VPN, their internet boundary is on the company firewall or virtual/cloud firewall.

heading: Wireless devices
text: Wireless devices (including wireless access points) are:

heading: Wireless devices
text: in scope if they can communicate with other devices via the internet

heading: Wireless devices
text: out of scope if it's not possible for an attacker to attack directly via the internet (the Cyber Essentials scheme isn’t concerned with attacks that can only be launched within the signal range of the wireless device)

heading: Wireless devices
text: out of scope if they are part of an ISP router at the home or remote location

heading: Cloud services
text: If your organisation’s data or services are hosted on cloud services, these services must be in scope.

heading: Cloud services
text: For cloud services, the applicant organisation is always responsible for ensuring all controls are implemented, but some of the controls can be implemented by the cloud service provider. Who implements which control depends on the type of cloud service. We consider three different types of cloud service:

heading: Cloud services
text: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) – the cloud provider delivers virtual servers and network equipment that, much like physical equipment, your organisation configures and manages. Examples of IaaS include Rackspace, Google Compute Engine, or Amazon EC2

heading: Cloud services
text: Platform as a Service (PaaS) – the cloud provider delivers and manages the underlying infrastructure, and your organisation provides and manages the applications. Examples of PaaS include Azure Web Apps and Amazon Web Services Lambda

heading: Cloud services
text: Software as a Service (SaaS) – the cloud provider delivers applications, and your organisation then configures the services. You must still make sure that the service is configured securely. Examples of SaaS include Microsoft 365, Dropbox and Gmail

heading: Cloud services
text: Who implements the controls will vary, depending how the cloud service is designed. The table below explains who might typically be expected to implement each control:

heading: Cloud services
text: In cases where the cloud provider implements one of the controls on your behalf, you must make sure that the cloud provider has committed to implementing this via contractual clauses or documents referenced by contract, such as security statements or privacy statements. Cloud providers will often explain how they implement security in documents published in their trust centres, referencing a ‘shared responsibility model.’

heading: Accounts used by third parties and managed infrastructure
text: All accounts that your organisation owns are in scope, even when those accounts are used by a third party, such as a supplier, contractor or Managed Service Provider (MSP) to manage or support your infrastructure.

heading: Accounts used by third parties and managed infrastructure
text: If you’re using externally managed services (such as remote administration), you must be able to confirm that the Cyber Essentials technical controls are being met and be able to demonstrate this in your assessment answers.

heading: Devices used by third parties
text: All end user devices your organisation owns that are loaned to a third party must be included in the assessment scope.

heading: Devices used by third parties
text: For devices not owned by your organisation, the table below explains what is in and out of scope:

heading: Devices used by third parties
text: For devices out of scope of the assessment, your organisation is still responsible for confirming that the devices interacting with organisational services and data are configured correctly. It's up to you how to achieve this, as it falls outside of the assessment scope.

heading: Software development
text: Publicly available commercial web applications (rather than apps developed in-house) are in scope by default. Bespoke and custom components of web applications are out of scope. The best way to mitigate vulnerabilities in applications is robust development and testing in line with commercial best practice. See the Software Security Code of Practice for further details.

heading: Introduction
text: All devices run network services to allow them to communicate with other devices and services. By restricting access to these services, you reduce your exposure to attacks. You can do this using firewalls or network devices with firewall functionality. For cloud services, you can achieve this using data flow policies.

heading: Introduction
text: A boundary firewall is a network device which can restrict the inbound and outbound network traffic to services on its network of computers and mobile devices. It can help protect against cyber attacks by implementing restrictions, known as ‘firewall rules,’ which can allow or block traffic depending on its source, destination and type of communication protocol.

heading: Introduction
text: Alternatively, if your organisation doesn't control the network to which a device connects, you must configure a software firewall on the device. This works in the same way as a boundary firewall but only protects the single device on which it’s configured. This approach allows for more tailored rules and means that the rules apply to the device wherever it's used. But you should note that this creates a greater administrative overhead when managing firewall rules.

heading: Requirements
text: You must protect every device in scope with a correctly configured firewall (or network device with firewall functionality).

heading: Requirements
text: Information: Most desktop and laptop operating systems now come with a software firewall pre-installed, we advise that these are turned on in preference to a third-party firewall application.

heading: Requirements
text: For all firewalls (or network devices with firewall functionality), your organisation must:

heading: Requirements
text: change default administrative passwords to a strong and unique password (see password-based authentication) – or disable remote administrative access entirely

heading: Requirements
text: prevent access to the administrative interface (used to manage firewall configuration) from the internet, unless there is a clear and documented business need, and the interface is protected by one of the following controls:

heading: Requirements
text: multi-factor authentication (see MFA details below)

heading: Requirements
text: an IP allow list that limits access to a small range of trusted addresses combined with a properly managed password authentication approach

heading: Requirements
text: block unauthenticated inbound connections by default

heading: Requirements
text: ensure inbound firewall rules are approved and documented by an authorised person, and include the business need in the documentation

heading: Requirements
text: remove or disable unnecessary firewall rules, when they are no longer needed

heading: Requirements
text: Make sure you use a software firewall on devices which are used on untrusted networks, such as public wifi hotspots.

heading: Introduction
text: The default configurations of computers and network devices aren’t always secure. Standard out-of-the-box configurations often include one or more weak points such as: an administrative account with a pre-set, publicly known default password or without multi-factor authentication enabled; pre-enabled but unnecessary user accounts (sometimes with special access privileges); pre-installed but unnecessary applications or services

heading: Introduction
text: These default installations can allow attackers to gain unauthorised access to your organisation’s sensitive information. But by applying some simple technical controls when installing computers and network devices, you can minimise vulnerabilities and protect against common types of attack.

heading: Computers and network devices
text: Your organisation must proactively manage your computers and network devices. You must regularly:

heading: Computers and network devices
text: remove and disable unnecessary user accounts (such as guest accounts and administrative accounts that won’t be used)

heading: Computers and network devices
text: change any default or guessable account passwords (see password-based authentication)

heading: Computers and network devices
text: remove or disable unnecessary software (including applications, system utilities and network services)

heading: Computers and network devices
text: disable any auto-run feature which allows file execution without user authorisation (such as when they are downloaded)

heading: Computers and network devices
text: ensure users are authenticated before allowing them access to organisational data or services

heading: Computers and network devices
text: ensure appropriate device locking controls (see ‘device unlocking’, below) for users that are physically present

heading: Device unlocking credentials
text: If a device requires a user’s physical presence to access a device’s services (such as logging on to a laptop or unlocking a mobile phone), a credential such as a biometric, password or PIN must be in place before a user can gain access to the services.

heading: Device unlocking credentials
text: You must protect your chosen authentication method (which can be biometric authentication, password or PIN) against brute-force attacks. When it's possible to configure, you should apply one of the following:

heading: Device unlocking credentials
text: ‘throttling' the rate of attempts, so that the length of time the user must wait between attempts increases with each unsuccessful attempt. You should allow no more than 10 guesses in 5 minutes

heading: Device unlocking credentials
text: locking devices after no more than 10 unsuccessful attempts

heading: Device unlocking credentials
text: When the vendor doesn't allow you to configure the above, use the vendor’s default setting.

heading: Device unlocking credentials
text: Technical controls must be used to manage the quality of credentials. If credentials are just to unlock a device, use a minimum password or PIN length of at least 6 characters. When the device unlocking credentials are also used for authentication, you must apply the full password requirements to the credentials described in User Access Controls.

heading: Introduction
text: Any device that runs software can contain security flaws, known as vulnerabilities.

heading: Introduction
text: Vulnerabilities are regularly discovered in all sorts of software. Once discovered, malicious individuals or groups move quickly to misuse (or ‘exploit’) vulnerabilities to attack computers and networks.

heading: Introduction
text: Product vendors provide fixes for vulnerabilities identified in products that they still support, in the form of patches, security updates, registry fixes, scripts, configuration changes or any other mechanism prescribed by the vendor to fix a known vulnerability. These may be made available to customers immediately or on a regular release schedule (perhaps monthly).

heading: Requirements
text: You must make sure that all software in scope is kept up to date. All software on in-scope devices must:

heading: Requirements
text: be licensed and supported

heading: Requirements
text: be removed from devices when it becomes unsupported, or removed from scope by using a defined sub-set that prevents all traffic to or from the internet

heading: Requirements
text: have automatic updates enabled where possible

heading: Requirements
text: be updated, including vulnerability fixes, within 14 days* of release, where:

heading: Requirements
text: the update fixes vulnerabilities described by the vendor as ‘critical’ or ‘high risk’

heading: Requirements
text: the update addresses vulnerabilities with a CVSS v3 base score of 7 or above

heading: Requirements
text: there are no details of the level of vulnerabilities that the update fixes provided by the vendor

heading: Requirements
text: Please note: For optimum security we strongly recommend (but it’s not mandatory) that all released updates are applied within 14 days of release.

heading: Requirements
text: *It's important that updates are applied as soon as possible. 14 days is considered a reasonable period to be able to implement this requirement. Any longer would constitute a serious security risk while a shorter period may not be practical.

heading: Requirements
text: Information: If the vendor uses different terms to describe the severity of vulnerabilities, see the precise definition in the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). For the purposes of the Cyber Essentials scheme, ‘critical’ or ‘high risk’ vulnerabilities are those with a CVSS v3 base score of 7 or above, or are identified by the vendor as 'critical or high risk'.

heading: Requirements
text: Caution: Some vendors release security updates for multiple issues with differing severity levels as a single update. If such an update covers any ‘critical’ or ‘high risk’ issues then it must be installed within 14 days.

heading: Introduction
text: Every active user account in your organisation facilitates access to devices and applications, and to sensitive business information. By making sure that only authorised individuals have user accounts, and that they're only granted as much access as they need to carry out their role, you reduce the risk of information being stolen or damaged.

heading: Introduction
text: Compared to normal user accounts, accounts with special access privileges have enhanced access to devices, applications and information. If these accounts are compromised, an attacker could take advantage of their greater access to corrupt information on a large scale, disrupt business processes or gain unauthorised access to other devices in the organisation.

heading: Introduction
text: Administrative accounts are especially highly privileged, for example. These accounts typically allow the user to: execute software that can make significant and security-related changes to the operating system; make changes to the operating system for some or all users; create new accounts and allocate privileges

heading: Introduction
text: All types of administrators will have this kind of account, including domain administrators and local administrators.

heading: Introduction
text: This is important because if a user opens a malicious URL or email attachment, the malware would typically be executed with the same privilege level of the user’s account. This is why it’s important to take special care allocating and using privileged accounts.

heading: Requirements
text: Your organisation must be in control of your user accounts and the access privileges that allow access to your organisational data and services. It’s important to note that this also includes third party accounts – for example, accounts used by your support services. You also need to understand how user accounts authenticate and manage the authentication accordingly.

heading: Requirements
text: This means your organisation must:

heading: Requirements
text: have in place a process to create and approve user accounts

heading: Requirements
text: authenticate users with unique credentials before granting access to applications or devices

heading: Requirements
text: remove or disable user accounts when they’re no longer required (for example, when a user leaves the organisation or after a defined period of account inactivity)

heading: Requirements
text: implement MFA, where available – authentication to cloud services must always use MFA

heading: Requirements
text: use separate accounts to perform administrative activities only (no emailing, web browsing or other standard user activities that may expose administrative privileges to avoidable risks)

heading: Requirements
text: remove or disable special access privileges when no longer required (when a member of staff changes role, for example)

heading: Passwordless authentication
text: Passwordless authentication is a method of verifying identity without using traditional passwords.

heading: Passwordless authentication
text: Common examples of passwordless authentication include:

heading: Passwordless authentication
text: Passkeys: Passwordless login technology based on public-key cryptography used to securely authenticate a user. This includes FIDO2 authenticators which are considered as Passkeys. FIDO2 authenticators are regarded as MFA because user authentication is performed. FIDO2 is a set of standards that define cryptographic authentication using public key credentials and protocols to provide more secure alternatives to passwords for accessing online services

heading: Passwordless authentication
text: Biometric authentication: Uses biological traits of the user such as fingerprints or facial features to confirm their identity

heading: Passwordless authentication
text: Security keys or tokens: Physical hardware devices such as USB security keys or smart cards

heading: Passwordless authentication
text: Push notifications: A prompt on a smartphone to approve or deny a login attempt

heading: Passwordless authentication
text: One-time codes: Temporary codes are sent via email, SMS, or a mobile app

heading: Passwordless authentication
text: This helps to avoid many of the problems with traditional passwords which can be forgotten, stolen, or brute-forced.

heading: Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
text: As well as providing an extra layer of security for passwords that aren’t protected by the other technical controls, you should always use multi-factor authentication to give administrative accounts extra security, and accounts that are accessible from the internet.

heading: Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
text: The password element of the multi-factor authentication approach must have a password length of at least 8 characters, with no maximum length restrictions.

heading: Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
text: There are four types of additional factor to consider:

heading: Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
text: a managed/enterprise device

heading: Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
text: an app on a trusted device

heading: Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
text: a physically separate token

heading: Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
text: a known or trusted account

heading: Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
text: Additional factors should be chosen so that they are usable and accessible. You might need to carry out user testing to decide what is best for your users. For more information see NCSC’s guidance on MFA.

heading: Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
text: Information: SMS is not the most secure type of MFA but still offers a huge advantage over not using any MFA at all. Any multi-factor authentication is better than not having it at all. However, if there are alternatives available that will work for your situation, we recommend you use these instead of SMS.

heading: Password-based authentication
text: All user accounts require the user to authenticate.

heading: Password-based authentication
text: Where authentication is carried out using a password, you should put in place the following protective measures:

heading: Password-based authentication
text: Passwords are protected against brute-force password guessing by implementing at least one of:

heading: Password-based authentication
text: multi-factor authentication (see above)

heading: Password-based authentication
text: ‘throttling' the rate of attempts, so that the length of time the user must wait between attempts increases with each unsuccessful attempt. You should allow no more than 10 guesses in 5 minutes

heading: Password-based authentication
text: locking devices after no more than 10 unsuccessful attempts

heading: Password-based authentication
text: Use technical controls to manage the quality of passwords. This will include one of the following:

heading: Password-based authentication
text: Using multi-factor authentication (see above)

heading: Password-based authentication
text: A minimum password length of at least 12 characters, with no maximum length restrictions

heading: Password-based authentication
text: A minimum password length of at least 8 characters, with no maximum length restrictions and use automatic blocking of common passwords using a deny list

heading: Password-based authentication
text: Support users to choose unique passwords for their work accounts by:

heading: Password-based authentication
text: educating people about avoiding common passwords, such as a pet's name, common keyboard patterns or passwords they have used elsewhere. This could include teaching people to use the password generator feature built into some password managers

heading: Password-based authentication
text: encouraging people to choose longer passwords by promoting the use of multiple words (a minimum of three) to create a password (such as the NCSC’s guidance on using three random words)

heading: Password-based authentication
text: providing usable secure storage for passwords (for example a password manager or secure locked cabinet) with clear information about how and when it can be used

heading: Password-based authentication
text: not enforcing regular password expiry

heading: Password-based authentication
text: not enforcing password complexity requirements

heading: Password-based authentication
text: You should also make sure there is an established process in place to change passwords promptly if you know or suspect a password or account has been compromised.

heading: Introduction
text: Malware, such as computer viruses, worms and ransomware, is software that has been written and distributed deliberately to perform malicious actions. Potential sources include: malicious email attachments, downloads (including those from application stores), and direct installation of unauthorised software.

heading: Introduction
text: If a system is infected, your organisation is likely to suffer from problems like malfunctioning systems, data loss, or onward infection that goes unseen until it causes harm elsewhere.

heading: Introduction
text: You can largely avoid the potential for harm by: preventing malware from being delivered to devices; preventing malware from running on devices

heading: Requirements
text: You must make sure that a malware protection mechanism is active on all devices in scope. For each device, you must use at least one of the options listed below. In most modern products these options are built into the software supplied. Alternatively, you can purchase products from a third-party provider. In all cases the software must be active, kept up to date in accordance with the vendor’s instructions, and configured to work as detailed below:

heading: Anti-malware software
text: Anti-malware software (option for in scope devices running Windows or MacOS including servers, desktop computers, laptops) If you use anti-malware software to protect your device it must be configured to:

heading: Anti-malware software
text: be updated in line with vendor recommendations

heading: Anti-malware software
text: prevent malware from running

heading: Anti-malware software
text: prevent the execution of malicious code

heading: Anti-malware software
text: prevent connections to malicious websites over the internet

heading: Application allow listing
text: Application allow listing (option for all in scope devices) Only approved applications, restricted by code signing, are allowed to execute on devices. You must:

heading: Application allow listing
text: actively approve such applications before deploying them to devices

heading: Application allow listing
text: maintain a current list of approved applications, users must not be able to install any application that is unsigned or has an invalid signature

heading: Zero trust and Cyber Essentials
text: Network architecture is changing. More services are moving to the cloud and use of Software as a Service (SaaS) continues to grow.

heading: Zero trust and Cyber Essentials
text: At the same time, many organisations are embracing flexible working, which means lots of different device types may connect to your systems from many locations. It's also increasingly common for organisations to share data with their partners and guest users, which requires more granular access control policies.

heading: Zero trust and Cyber Essentials
text: Zero trust architecture is designed to cope with these changing conditions by enabling an improved user experience for remote access and data sharing.

heading: Zero trust and Cyber Essentials
text: A zero trust architecture is an approach to system design where inherent trust in the network is removed. Instead the network is assumed to be hostile, and each access request is verified based on an access policy. Confidence in a request is achieved by building context, which relies on strong authentication, authorisation, device health, and value of the data being accessed.

heading: Zero trust and Cyber Essentials
text: As organisations move towards zero trust architecture models, we have considered it in this context, and are confident that implementing the technical controls doesn't prevent you using a zero trust architecture as defined by the NCSC guidance.
